title: Can business learn from computer games?

paragraphs.text: Tomorrow's business landscape could be alien territory for today's business leaders. In the future, important decision-making will be distributed throughout the organization, to enable people to respond rapidly to change. A lot of work will be done by global teams – partly composed of people from outside the institution, over whom a leader has no formal authority – that are assembled for a single project and then disbanded. Collaboration within these geographically diverse groups will, by necessity, occur mainly through digital rather than face-to-face interaction. What on earth will leadership look like in such a world? Suspend your skepticism for a moment when we say that the answers may be found among the exploding space stations and grotesque monsters of online games.

Despite their fantasy settings, these online play worlds in many ways resemble the coming business environment we have described. While it is true that leading 25 members of a guild, as a team, in a six-hour raid on a fantasy fortress is hardly the same as running a complex global organization – the stakes are much lower, of course – you should not dismiss online games as just play. The best games differ from traditional video games, much as universities do from one-room schoolhouses. In fact, online games are the richest interactive environments in which thousands of players collaborate with and compete against one another in a visually three-dimensional virtual world.

The organizational and strategic challenges facing players who serve as game leaders are familiar to business leaders. Both must recruit, motivate and retain talented and culturally diverse team members; identify and capitalize on the organization's competitive advantage; analyze multiple streams of constantly changing and often incomplete data in order to make quick decisions that have wide-ranging and sometimes long-lasting effects. But these management challenges are heightened in online games, because an organization must be built and sustained with a volunteer workforce in a fluid and digitally mediated environment.

Watching how leadership works in online games isn't easy: to see the best players in action, you need skills that allow you to participate at the highest levels of play, and those can take 400 to 500 hours to acquire. IT and games consultancy Seriosity carried out a study of leadership in games, using a team of a half-dozen veteran players, with more than 50,000 hours of cumulative experience, to watch and record the actions of leaders in this setting. The eight-month study also included interviews with more than a dozen prominent gamers about their leadership endeavors in this arena.

A number of Seriosity's findings about the future of business leadership were unanticipated. For one, individuals who would never be identified as 'high-potentials' for real-world management training take on positions of responsibility in games. Even more provocative was the finding that successful leadership in online games has less to do with the attributes of individual leaders than with the game environment. Furthermore, some characteristics of that environment, for example rewarding team members for their success as soon as a project is completed, perhaps in a nonmonetary form, suggest how business leadership is likely to evolve.

Perhaps the most striking aspect of leadership in online games is the way in which leaders naturally switch roles, directing others one minute and taking orders the next. Put another way, leadership in games is a task, not an identity. Someone leading a guild may grow weary of the stress and hand off to a successor, then resume later as a rank-and-file member of the group. Notably, choices about who will lead and who will follow are often made organically by the group, without some higher authority.

Trial and error also play a big role in accomplishing online game tasks. Failure, instead of being viewed as a career killer, is accepted as a frequent and necessary antecedent to success. Frequent risk-taking allows players to practice the art of weighing odds calmly in uncertain environments. In the real world, organizations can help prepare leaders by fostering a culture in which failure is tolerated. They can expose leaders to risk by mimicking the structure of games, breaking down big challenges into small projects. Failure, after all, is clearly more palatable for the individual and more affordable for the organization when its effects are limited, rather than on a larger scale.

Another difference between play and reality is that gamers operate through characters, or avatars, that they have adopted and personalized for the game, and that disguise their real-world identities. It's clear from laboratory research that players are highly invested psychologically in their avatars. That passionate attachment, coupled with the ability to act through their alter ego, makes heated disagreements both common and accepted.

Most research on leadership selection and development focuses on people's backgrounds and natural talents, the assumption being that expertise resides within the individual. The Seriosity study provided an arrestingly different view: perhaps the right environment is what really matters, whoever the leader happens to be. This concept, which seems to be absent from the academic and professional literature about leadership, wasn't something that the consultancy set out to prove. The notion arose from the experienced gamers on the research team, who were puzzled by Seriosity's initial preoccupation with the individual qualities of game leaders: 'If you want better leadership,' they asked, 'why not change the game instead of the leaders?'

questions.prompt: According to the first paragraph, which of the following describes the future business environment?

options.text: Working groups will be temporary.
People will travel more frequently.
Leaders will manage larger groups of people.
Smaller companies will dominate the business world.

questions.prompt: In the second paragraph, why does the writer mention universities?

options.text: to show that video games reflect contemporary life
to show that online games are more educational than traditional games
to show how much the best online games have advanced
to show why online games represent the future of business

questions.prompt: What difference between games and business is mentioned in the third paragraph?

options.text: the difficulty of decision-making
the nature of the people's commitment
the amount of information to be processed
the need for team members to come from a range of backgrounds

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a feature of the study conducted by Seriosity?

options.text: Researchers played online games for 400 to 500 hours.
Two companies created an online business training tool
Researchers spent eight months observing experienced gamers.
Gamers were given leadership roles in a company for eight months.

questions.prompt: On the topic of failure, what does the writer say that organisations need to do?

options.text: allow staff to fail in small projects without penalty
reduce the responsibilities of workers who fail in a project
provide extra training for people who fail in a project
avoid giving inexperienced staff projects they might fail in

questions.prompt: In the final paragraph, what aspect of the study puzzled the experienced gamers in the research team?

options.text: the limitations of the game they were asked to play
the focus on people rather than on the game itself
the limited skills required to play the game
the tasks they were asked to perform

groups.title: Seriosity's research findings
content: People may be effective in {{33}} in games that they would not be considered suitable for at work, though their success may reflect the game environment rather than their individual {{34}} . Success in games provides players with immediate rewards, a practice that businesses may need to adopt. In a game, being leader is likely to continue for a more {{35}} period than at work, and changes of leader are often {{36}} decisions.
